content: The genus Aesculus consists of 20 to 25 species of deciduous trees and shrubs that are native to the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Among these, 7 to 10 species are native to North America, while 13 to 15 species are found in Eurasia. Additionally, several natural hybrids exist within this genus. Historically, these plants were classified under their own family, Hippocastanaceae, which was typically monogeneric. However, genetic studies have led to the reclassification of this family, along with the Aceraceae (maples and Dipteronia), into the soapberry family, Sapindaceae. In North America, species of Aesculus are commonly referred to as Buckeyes, while in Eurasia, they are known as Horse-chestnuts. Some species are also called White Chestnut or Red Chestnut, as seen in certain Bach flower remedies. In Britain, these trees are colloquially referred to as Conker trees due to their association with the traditional game of conkers. The term Horse-chestnut is hyphenated to distinguish it from true chestnuts (Castanea, family Fagaceae). This name is also sometimes written as Horse Chestnut or Horsechestnut. One of the most widely cultivated species, Aesculus hippocastanum (Common Horse-chestnut), is often simply referred to as Horse-chestnut. The genus name Aesculus was assigned by Linnaeus, deriving from the Roman term for an edible acorn. The prefix horse in Horse-chestnut does not imply suitability as horse fodder but rather refers to strength or inedibility, as the word horse historically connoted power or robustness. The name Buckeye originates from the resemblance of the seed to the brown eye of a male deer (buck), while Horse-chestnut refers to the seed's external similarity to a chestnut, despite being inedible. Buckeye trees typically bloom in summer, whereas Horse-chestnuts flower in late spring. Aesculus species are woody plants that range in height from 4 to 35 meters, depending on the species. They are characterized by stout shoots with resinous, often sticky buds, and opposite, palmately compound leaves that are frequently large, reaching up to 65 cm in width in species like the Japanese Horse-chestnut (Aesculus turbinata). The flowers are showy and insect-pollinated, with a single petal that is fouror five-lobed, though these petals are fused at the base. Flowering begins after the accumulation of 80 to 110 growing degree days. The nut is typically globose and encased in a green or brown husk, which may contain one or, less commonly, two nuts. When two nuts are present, they are flattened on one side. The attachment point of the nut to the husk is marked by a large, circular, whitish scar. The husk may have scattered soft spines in some species, while others are spineless. It splits into three sections to release the nut. The most widely recognized species of Aesculus is the Common Horse-chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), which is native to a small region in the Balkans of southeastern Europe but is now cultivated extensively across temperate regions worldwide. Another notable species is the Yellow Buckeye (Aesculus flava, synonym A. octandra), valued as an ornamental tree for its yellow flowers, though it is less commonly planted. Among the smaller species, the Bottlebrush Buckeye (Aesculus parviflora) is an unusual and striking flowering shrub. Several other species within the genus are also used as ornamental plants, and numerous horticultural hybrids have been developed. One prominent hybrid is the Red Horse-chestnut (Aesculus × carnea), a cross between A. hippocastanum and A. pavia. These plants are generally low-maintenance, but a recently identified leaf-mining moth (Cameraria ohridella) has caused significant damage in parts of Europe, leading to premature leaf drop and unsightly brown blotches on the leaves. These symptoms can be mistaken for damage caused by the leaf fungus Guignardia aesculi, which is also common but typically less severe. The Common Horse-chestnut also serves as a food source for the larvae of the Sycamore moth. Another issue affecting Aesculus species in parts of northwestern Europe and North America is bleeding canker disease. The nuts of Aesculus species contain high levels of a saponin-class toxin called aesculin, which is toxic to many animals, including humans, as it induces hemolysis (the destruction of red blood cells). However, the toxin can be removed by leaching the pulverized nuts in multiple changes of boiling water, yielding a starchy porridge that was once a significant food source for some Native American tribes. Certain animals, such as deer and squirrels, are resistant to the toxin and can consume the nuts without harm. Interestingly, aesculin is a natural pH indicator that fluoresces blue under UV light in acidic conditions. Crushed buckeye nuts have historically been used by poachers to kill fish in lakes, making them easier to catch. The California Buckeye (Aesculus californica) is known to produce nectar that is toxic to honeybees, although other native bee species in the region are unaffected. Other buckeye species are believed to have similar effects, but the impact is mitigated by the trees' relatively low density in any given area. The wood of Aesculus species is pale whitish-brown, soft, and of limited use, primarily employed in the production of inexpensive furniture, boxes, and firewood. In Britain and Ireland, the game of conkers, which involves the seeds of Horse-chestnuts, remains a popular childhood activity. In some cultures, the buckeye tree is considered a symbol of good luck. The Mexican Buckeye, while related to Aesculus, belongs to a separate genus, Ungnadia. In homeopathic medicine, Aesculus is used to treat pain in the sacroiliac region and rectal pain.
